title: Aero 311
summary: Aero Flight 311 crashed near Kvevlax, Finland, while in approach for landing. The investigation revealed that both pilots were intoxicated: Captain Hattinen had a blood alcohol content of 0.20 and First Officer Halme had 0.156. The pilots made a left turn, the aircraft slowed and went into a spin that could not be recovered, impacting the woods in a steep 70-degree turn.
probable_cause: The probable cause of the accident was determined to be pilot error when making a left turn. Neither pilot was in a fit state to fly. Hattinen had a blood alcohol content of 0.20 (2 ‰), while Halme had 0.156 (1.56 ‰). They had not slept well the previous night and had been drinking heavily.

factors.evidence: Autopsies revealed that Hattinen had a blood alcohol content of 0.20 (2 ‰), while Halme had 0.156 (1.56 ‰)
They had not slept well the previous night and had been drinking heavily
The pilots did not follow these regulations for the last 40 km, during which they flew below 100 m
Suddenly, the plane turned abruptly to the left. This slowed the plane and disrupted airflow significantly

the plane went into a spin. The last thing seen by eyewitnesses on the ground was that the pilots had turned the landing lights on before the plane crashed into the woods at 07:40:30 in a steep 70-degree turn
the plane crashed into the woods at 07:40:30 in a steep 70-degree turn

events.text: Flight took off from Kronoby Airport at 07:16, after delayed take-off preparations
Aircraft descending below 50 m in preparation for landing
Plane turned abruptly to the left, slowed, and disrupted airflow significantly
Plane went into a spin, pilots turned landing lights on, crashed into woods in steep 70-degree turn

notes: Investigation definitive; autopsies confirmed blood alcohol levels; remains deadliest aviation accident in Finnish history

title: Sabena 548
summary: Sabena Flight 548, a Boeing 707 flying from New York to Brussels, made two aborted landing attempts at Brussels Airport on 15 February 1961 after a small aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. On a third circuit the aircraft's bank angle gradually increased until it reached a near-vertical bank at 1,500 ft; it then leveled its wings, pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled nose-down into the ground near Berg, killing all 72 aboard and one person on the ground. Investigators could not conclusively determine the cause but believed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism, possibly involving the wing spoilers.
probable_cause: The exact cause was never fully determined. Authorities agreed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of a flight-control mechanism, probably a malfunction of the wing spoilers or, as the FAA believed, the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism.

factors.evidence: the FAA felt that the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism had failed
The airplane had been forced to cancel its final approach, as a small plane had not yet cleared the runway
the pilots were fighting for control of the aircraft, attempting to land despite a mechanical malfunction preventing a normal landing
the plane's bank angle gradually increased... pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled rapidly, nose-down

events.text: Near the runway threshold at a height of 900 ft, power was increased and the landing gear retracted after the approach was aborted because a small plane had not yet cleared the runway.
The 707 circled the airport and attempted to land on the adjoining Runway 25, which was not operational, but this second approach was also aborted.
Witnesses observed that the pilots were fighting for control of the aircraft, attempting to land despite a mechanical malfunction preventing a normal landing.
The plane's bank angle gradually increased until it had climbed to 1500 ft and was in a near vertical bank, then leveled its wings, pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled rapidly, nose-down.
The plane plunged into the ground less than two miles from the airport at 10:05 CET, and eyewitnesses said it exploded and burst into flames.

notes: Cause was never conclusively established; text presents FAA's stabilizer-failure hypothesis as the leading theory among several considered.

title: Viasa 897
summary: Flight 897 entered a spiral dive to the left a few minutes after takeoff from Lisbon during nighttime over the Atlantic and struck the sea at approximately 25 degrees nose-down. The pilot over-corrected to the right during the upset. The official investigation concluded it was not possible to establish the probable cause, though authorities suggested possible instrument failure or pilot distraction.

factors.evidence: The accident occurred at 01:15 UTC at nighttime.
The pilot was possibly distracted or misled by instrument failure, in particular artificial horizon.
The pilot over-corrected to the right during the spiral dive.
The aircraft entered a spiral dive to the left and struck the sea.

events.text: The aircraft lifted off from Lisbon at 01:15 UTC with a cloud base of 3700 ft.
A few minutes after takeoff the DC-8 entered a spiral dive to the left after sending two short messages to Air Traffic Control.
The pilot over-corrected to the right.
The aircraft struck the sea with a pitch angle of approximately 25 degrees nose down.

notes: Cause never determined; investigating authorities offered speculative hypotheses only

title: TWA 529
summary: TWA Flight 529, a Lockheed Constellation, took off from Midway Airport in Chicago at 02:00 CDT on 1 September 1961 bound for Los Angeles. Five minutes into climb at approximately 5,000 feet, the aircraft pitched violently upward and entered an aerodynamic stall from which the crew could not recover, crashing into terrain in Willowbrook, Illinois. Investigation revealed a critical 5/16-inch bolt had fallen out of the elevator boost linkage, and the aircraft's design prevented manual elevator control when under nose-down pressure.
probable_cause: Loss of an AN-175-21 nickel steel bolt from the parallelogram linkage of the elevator boost system, resulting in loss of control of the aircraft.

factors.evidence: A critical 5/16 inch AN-175-21 nickel steel bolt was missing in the elevator boost linkage mechanism, having fallen out prior to the accident
Without the bolt in place, the elevator in boost mode became uncontrollable
Design was such that continuous nose down pressure on elevators made shift to manual elevator control mechanically impossible
Aircraft suddenly pitched violently upwards resulting in accelerated stall
Crew unable to recover from stall after violent pitch up

events.text: Aircraft departed from runway 22 at Midway Airport bound for Las Vegas

Pilots attempted to revert to manual control but design prevented takeover under nose-down pressure
Aircraft crashed into terrain in Willowbrook, Dupage County, leaving 200 by 1,100 feet debris field

notes: Root cause clearly identified by CAB through wreckage analysis
Design deficiency prevented emergency recovery procedure
Led to FAA recommendation for elevator boost control redesign

title: Aerolíneas Argentinas 322
summary: Aerolíneas Argentinas Flight 322 crashed shortly after takeoff from Viracopos-Campinas Airport on November 23, 1961. The Comet 4 reached approximately 100 meters altitude before losing altitude and colliding with eucalyptus trees during dark night conditions. Investigation revealed the first officer was receiving in-flight instruction in the left seat and the captain failed to follow proper IFR procedures for night operations.
probable_cause: Failure to operate under IFR procedures during night weather conditions and failure to follow the prescribed climb procedure, compounded by inadequate supervision of the pilot under instruction.

factors.evidence: the first officer was seated in the left seat of the flight deck, which the investigators saw as an indication that he was receiving flight instruction
weather conditions at the time of the accident were dark night due to 7/8 broken stratocumulus at 400 m

title: Aeroflot 245
summary: Aeroflot Flight 245, an Ilyushin Il-18B, departed Moscow on December 17, 1961, climbing to cruising altitude of 8000 m at 630 km/h. At 15:59, while in level flight, the flight engineer inadvertently moved the flaps selector to full extension of 40 degrees, causing a large drag increase. The aircraft pitched over and entered a steep descent, with flap assemblies ripping from the wings during the dive.
probable_cause: The flight engineer inadvertently moved the flaps selector to full extension at cruising speed. The Il-18 lacked a mechanism to prevent accidental flap selector movement, which was found to be a contributing factor in the accident sequence. Due to high negative g-force during the dive, the crew could not reach the flap selector to retract the flaps.

factors.evidence: flight engineer inadvertently moved the flaps selector to full extension of 40 degrees
Il-18 did not have a mechanism to prevent accidental flap selector movement and this was found to be a contributing factor
aircraft pitched over and entered a steep descent with port and starboard flap assemblies ripped from wing

events.text: At 14:34 Moscow time the Il-18 departed Vnukovo International Airport and climbed to its cruising altitude of 8000 m.
At 15:47 the crew contacted ATC and gave a position report, then the flight again communicated with ATC at 15:52.
While in level flight cruising at 630 km/h the flight engineer inadvertently moved the flaps selector to full extension of 40 degrees.
At 16:00 the aircraft impacted the ground at very high speed with the landing gear retracted and at a pitch angle of 107 degrees.

notes: investigation clearly identified accidental flap extension as initiating cause
design deficiency in flap selector protection identified
lack of g-force protection mechanism contributed
